title: The Rue des Marchands to Bedloe's Island: the Refused Lighthouse and the Woman with the Torch
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Rue des Marchands and the Rue Vavin

stops.name: Colmar, rue des Marchands: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia agree on 2 August 1834, and the Musee Bartholdi places the birth at 30 rue des Marchands.
stops.campa: On the second of August a son is born in the merchant house at 30 rue des Marchands, in a town of half timbered gables where French is spoken over a German substrate. His father, Jean Charles, is a councillor of the prefecture; his mother, Augusta Charlotte Beysser, is a mayor's daughter out of Ribeauville. Colmar is a border town, and in his thirty seventh year the border will cross it and leave the town German. The house he is carried out of as an infant opens as a museum under his name eighteen years after his death.
suggested_refs: The house at 30 rue des Marchands, Colmar, later the Musee Bartholdi

stops.name: Colmar: the father dies and the widow decides
stops.date_confidence: year attested; fr.wikipedia gives Jean Charles Bartholdi 1791-1836, conseiller de prefecture. Month and day not established and defaulted to 01-01. The common compression of this death with the move to Paris is rejected here: fr.wikipedia places the move at the 1843 lycee enrolment, seven years later.
stops.campa: Jean Charles Bartholdi dies, and the household of a prefectural councillor becomes the household of a widow with sons. Augusta Charlotte does not remarry. She keeps the Colmar house and the accounts, and she decides what her younger boy is to become; every later step of his education is her arrangement and her money. The move to Paris that the biographies attach to this death does not follow it. Seven years pass in Colmar before she takes the boys anywhere, and she chooses the year herself.
suggested_refs: Augusta Charlotte Beysser (1801-1891), daughter of a mayor of Ribeauville

stops.name: Paris, Lycée Louis-le-Grand: the Alsatian boy enrolled
stops.date_confidence: year attested by fr.wikipedia for the enrolment; day and month not given and defaulted. The baccalaureat of 1852 is attested by both fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia. The claim that the family kept the Colmar house and returned each summer is museum-chronology tradition, not documented here.
stops.campa: The widow brings her sons to Paris and enters Auguste at the Lycee Louis-le-Grand on the rue Saint-Jacques, seven years after the funeral. He will take his baccalaureat here in 1852. Nothing in the school's record marks him out; what will matter is happening in the evenings, at drawing lessons his mother pays for. Colmar stays behind him as a summer address rather than a place he has left, and he will answer to it as home long after Paris has made him.
suggested_refs: The Lycee Louis-le-Grand, rue Saint-Jacques, Paris

stops.name: Paris, rue Chaptal: the atelier of Ary Scheffer
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the years c.1851-1853 come from standard biographies and Musee de la Vie Romantique records rather than a document. The tuition under Antoine Etex is attested but undated in reachable sources. The reading of Scheffer's teaching as the origin of Bartholdi's preoccupation with silhouette is interpretation, not a sourced statement of his.
stops.campa: He studies in the courtyard atelier of Ary Scheffer on the rue Chaptal, having already worked under Antoine Etex, and so learns sculpture from a painter. Scheffer teaches the Romantic vocabulary of gesture and drapery, and teaches that a figure carries its meaning in its outline before a viewer is close enough to read a face. Bartholdi works outward from the outline afterwards. He composes in profile, settles the silhouette before the modelling, and the raised arms of the next fifty years all begin as a shape drawn against the sky.
suggested_refs: Ary Scheffer's courtyard studio, rue Chaptal, now the Musee de la Vie Romantique
sources: Musee de la Vie Romantique records

stops.name: Paris: the Salon of 1853 and the Good Samaritan
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia; day and month defaulted. The venue is a stated gap: an earlier attribution to the Palais de l'Industrie is retracted as anachronistic, since that building was erected in 1855 and housed the Salon only from 1857. No reachable source names the 1853 Salon's location, so the coordinate is a Paris centre pin and nothing finer.
stops.campa: He submits a sculptural group, The Good Samaritan, to the Paris Salon, the annual gauntlet every French sculptor runs to be seen at all. He is nineteen and unknown to the jury, one submission among hundreds, with no patron behind him and nothing yet made larger than a room. The Salon habit outlasts his need for it; he keeps sending work long after New York harbour has made him famous enough not to. Where that year's jury sat is not recorded in any source reached here.
suggested_refs: The Good Samaritan, Bartholdi's first Salon submission, 1853

stops.name: Paris, rue Vavin: the studio his mother buys
stops.date_confidence: year attested by fr.wikipedia; month and day defaulted. The forty-year tenancy is given by fr.wikipedia and Musee Bartholdi archives as a round figure rather than a lease record.
stops.campa: His mother buys him a workshop on the rue Vavin, in Montparnasse, and he keeps it for forty years. Every colossus starts here at arm's length, a clay woman with a lamp small enough to turn on a table, before anyone enlarges her ninety times. Fashions turn over outside the door, realism and then Art Nouveau, and Bartholdi stays with a grand allegorical mode other sculptors are already calling old. He gives the room up only in the eighteen nineties, when the harbour statue has been standing for years.
suggested_refs: Bartholdi's workshop on the rue Vavin, Montparnasse, kept from 1853

segments.name: Egypt, and the Measure of the Colossal

stops.name: Alexandria: the landing with the painters
stops.date_confidence: the voyage is attested for 1855-1856 by en.wikipedia, fr.wikipedia and Bartholdi's own 1885 account, which names Gerome and Belly among his companions. Month and day of the landing are not recorded and are defaulted. Itinerary contradiction flagged: en.wikipedia says Egypt and Yemen, fr.wikipedia says Egypte et Arabie.
stops.campa: He lands at Alexandria in a party of French orientalist painters, Jean Leon Gerome among them, with a sketchbook and no commission. It is his first sight of a country that has been building to outlast its builders for four thousand years. He is twenty one and travelling for pleasure: no patron sends him, no work is expected of him, and he draws whatever stands in front of him. Thirty years later, writing from the far side of the Atlantic, he dates his whole taste for sculpture on the colossal scale to this coast.
stops.quote: When I was twenty years old I traveled in Egypt with the painters Gerome and Belly, and several other friends, and I may say that this country had a very considerable effect upon my taste for sculpture
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), English translation, Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The 1855-56 Egyptian sketchbooks and travel photographs, Musee Bartholdi, Colmar
sources: Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (1885)
National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Giza: the pyramids and the Sphinx
stops.date_confidence: the Giza leg is attested by the NPS official history and standard biographies; no date within the 1855-56 voyage is recorded, so the year is used and month and day defaulted. The specific derivation of Bartholdi's rule of long-distance legibility from Giza is an interpretive commonplace repeated by the NPS, not a documented statement of his.
stops.campa: At Giza he stands under the pyramids and before the Sphinx. The scale is not simply larger than a French monument; it is a different category of object, built to be read from the horizon and to hold that reading at every distance in between. He works out the rule here and repeats it for fifty years: a colossus must carry an expression a mile off and survive inspection at arm's length. No monument in France is designed to be seen from a boat two hours away.
suggested_refs: The Great Sphinx and the Giza pyramid field
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Abu Simbel: the seated colossi of Ramesses
stops.date_confidence: attested for the voyage by the NPS official history; the year within the 1855-56 trip is a reasonable placement for the southern Nile leg but is not documented, and month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: Travelling south along the Nile he reaches Abu Simbel, where four seated Ramesses cut from the cliff have watched the river for three thousand years. They sit at the old southern threshold of Egypt, the first thing arriving traffic meets and the last thing it passes. When he later draws a robed woman with a lifted light at the mouth of a canal, and later still at the mouth of a harbour, he is repeating this placement. The figures here do not stand in a square or a garden. They stand on a border, facing whoever crosses it.
suggested_refs: The rock-cut colossi of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Aden: the far end of the sketchbook
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Musee Bartholdi collection notes describe Egypt-Yemen sketches of 1855-56 and en.wikipedia names Yemen, but no reachable source documents an Aden itinerary in detail, and fr.wikipedia says Arabia instead. The stop is carried as tradition, and the date is a default within the voyage years.
stops.campa: The tour runs past Egypt to Aden on the Yemeni coast, an unusual reach for a French sculptor of his generation. Watercolours and sketches survive from this end of the journey, an artist collecting faces, costume and light rather than commissions. Nothing is built here and nothing was asked for. What he carries home is a visual vocabulary of the exotic and the enormous, which he spends five decades converting into bronze and hammered copper on two continents, most of it for clients who never left Europe.
suggested_refs: Watercolours and sketches of the 1855-56 Egypt and Yemen journey, Musee Bartholdi

segments.name: The First Monument and the Refused Lighthouse

stops.name: Colmar, Champ-de-Mars: General Rapp unveiled
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia gives the inauguration on the Champ-de-Mars at Colmar, 31 August 1856.
stops.campa: His first great public commission goes up in his own city: a bronze General Jean Rapp, the Alsatian who served Napoleon as aide de camp, unveiled on the Champ de Mars at Colmar on the thirty first of August. Bartholdi is twenty two. The statue announces the register he will work in for the rest of his life, a single upright figure built to be looked up at, carrying a nation's memory in its posture rather than its face. Colmar applauds one of its own. The commission that defines him is fifteen years off.
suggested_refs: The bronze General Jean Rapp, Place Rapp, Colmar

stops.name: Glatigny: the sentence at Laboulaye's dinner
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction resting on a single retrospective witness. Bartholdi's 1885 pamphlet reports the dinner and quotes Laboulaye verbatim twenty years after the fact; no contemporaneous record was reached, and part of the scholarship treats the evening as a founding legend rather than a documented meeting. Month and day defaulted; the coordinate for Laboulaye's house at Glatigny near Versailles is approximate.
stops.campa: At a dinner in Edouard de Laboulaye's house the talk turns to the American republic, which the jurist admires, studies and has never seen. Laboulaye says that if a monument to American independence were ever raised it ought to be raised by the two nations together. Bartholdi, a decade younger and with a rejected Egyptian lighthouse still ahead of him, writes the sentence down and keeps it. Twenty one years pass between the remark at that table and the fog over Bedloe's Island, and he credits this evening for all of them.
stops.quote: if a monument were to be built in America as a memorial to their independence, I should think it very natural if it were built by united effort, if it were a common work of both nations
stops.quote_source: Edouard de Laboulaye, quoted verbatim by Bartholdi recounting the 1865 dinner at Glatigny, in The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: Edouard de Laboulaye's house at Glatigny, near Versailles
sources: Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (1885)

stops.name: Port Said: Egypt and the light refused
stops.date_confidence: the project and its refusal are attested by en.wikipedia, the NPS and Bartholdi's own 1885 account; month and day defaulted. The project's title is contested three ways and not resolved: fr.wikipedia gives L'Egypte eclairant l'Orient, en.wikipedia gives Egypt Carrying the Light to Asia, the NPS gives Egypt or Progress Carrying the Light to Asia.
stops.campa: He comes back to Egypt with a proposal in hand: a colossal robed woman at the northern mouth of the newly cut canal, a lantern raised over her head, lighthouse and monument in one body. He puts the project before the Khedive Ismail Pasha, who judges it too costly and declines; an ordinary lighthouse by Francois Coignet goes up at Port Said instead. The rejected figure stays in his sketchbooks. It changes its name and its nation, and seventeen years later it is standing in a harbour on the far side of the Atlantic.
stops.quote: At this period I was expecting to execute a statue of Egypt for the Suez Lighthouse. I even laid before Ismail Pacha a project.
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), English translation, Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The rejected Suez lighthouse project, and Francois Coignet's lighthouse built at Port Said instead
sources: Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (1885)
National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

segments.name: The Year of the Defeat, and the First Crossing

stops.name: Colmar: the province lost
stops.date_confidence: his service as a squadron leader of the National Guard is attested by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia; that he personally organised or joined the local defence of Colmar is reconstruction repeated by museum material and general biographies, not traced here to a document. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: War with Prussia comes into Alsace, and Bartholdi, thirty six, puts down the modelling tools and serves as a squadron leader of the National Guard. He is defending streets he sketched as a boy. Within the year Alsace is annexed by the German Empire and Colmar becomes foreign soil to the French state he goes on serving; his birthplace and his citizenship come apart and stay apart for good. He never stops calling himself Alsatian. For the rest of his life he is a Frenchman who crosses a state frontier to visit the house he was born in.
suggested_refs: The annexation of Alsace to the German Empire, 1871

stops.name: Autun: liaison to Garibaldi's Army of the Vosges
stops.date_confidence: the attachment to Garibaldi is attested by both wikipedias; fr.wikipedia calls him aide de camp but specifies his function as government liaison agent for supply, and the specified function is used here. The Dijon anchoring found in earlier accounts is corrected: per en.wikipedia 'Army of the Vosges', Dijon was already surrendered when Garibaldi arrived in November 1870, the army fell back on a besieged Autun, re-entered Dijon in January 1871 and lost it again on 1 February 1871. Day and month defaulted.
stops.campa: Attached to Giuseppe Garibaldi's Army of the Vosges, the sculptor spends the war's last months as a government liaison agent, moving supply between French authorities and a Piedmontese revolutionary commanding volunteers for a republic not his own. The army has no settled seat: Dijon is already surrendered when Garibaldi arrives, Autun is besieged, Dijon is retaken in January and lost again in February. His war is paperwork, and the front it serves never holds one town for a full month.
suggested_refs: The Army of the Vosges under Garibaldi, Autun and Dijon, winter 1870-1871

stops.name: New York Harbor: the plan made clear
stops.date_confidence: the 1871 crossing is attested by the NPS, en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia, the last of which frames it specifically as site selection. The month of arrival was not established and is defaulted. The coordinate is a harbour pin, not a landing place.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic for the first time carrying letters of introduction and an idea with no site, no money and no client. Sailing up through the Narrows he sees the harbour open, ships at every angle, a city on one bank and a low island in the middle water, and the vague monument in his head acquires a place to stand. He is thirty six and has been imagining a colossus for sixteen years. The distinction he draws afterwards is exact: the conception was formed on the voyage, the plan became clear at the sight of the harbour.
stops.quote: In the course of the voyage I formed some conceptions of a plan of a monument, but I can say that at the view of the harbor of New York the definite plan was first clear to my eyes.
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), English translation, Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The Narrows and the upper bay of New York, entered June 1871
sources: Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (1885)
National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Bedloe's Island: the site chosen
stops.date_confidence: attested by the NPS and by Bartholdi's own account; day and month not recorded and defaulted. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from gustave_eiffel.journey.json, where the same island carries 40.6892 / -74.0445.
stops.campa: He fixes on Bedloe's Island, a star shaped fort on federal ground in the middle of the water, and the reasoning is political before it is aesthetic: land belonging to no single state suits a monument meant to belong to the whole union rather than to New York. Every ship entering the port must pass it. He makes a watercolour of a robed woman standing on the fort's wall with her arm up, which is the entire project at this date, one sheet of paper and a conviction stated aloud to whoever will listen.
stops.quote: Yes, in this very place shall be raised the Statue of Liberty, grand as the idea which it embodies, radiant upon the two worlds.
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), English translation, Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: Fort Wood on Bedloe's Island, the star fort whose walls became the pedestal's base
sources: Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (1885)
National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Niagara Falls: the cross country tour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The 1871 cross-country tour and the presentations to Grant and others are attested by Bartholdi's own 1885 account; the Niagara stop in particular is traditional and was not confirmed in any primary source reached here. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The tour runs across the continent by rail, Bartholdi selling an unbuilt statue to anyone who will hear him out: President Grant, Peter Cooper, Cyrus Field, Agassiz, newspapermen. At Niagara he adds the falls to a private catalogue of things too large to take in at a glance, beside the pyramids and the seated kings of Abu Simbel. He goes home more certain and no richer. The money is still years away on both sides of the ocean, and the American subscription has not yet begun at all.
stops.quote: Among the notabilities to whom I had the honor of being presented I will mention General Grant, President of the United States at that time, General Meade, General Sheridan, Mr. Peter Cooper, Mr. Cyrus Field, Mr. Agassiz, Colonel Forney and other members of the press.
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), on the 1871 American tour, Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The 1871 American tour, undertaken with letters of introduction from Edouard de Laboulaye
sources: Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (1885)

stops.name: Paris, rue Cadet: the lodge Alsace-Lorraine
stops.date_confidence: the year of his initiation into the lodge Alsace-Lorraine is attested by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia; day and month defaulted. The coordinate is reconstruction: the lodge's own 1875 meeting address was not established, and the Grand Orient de France building on the rue Cadet is used as an approximate Paris masonic pin.
stops.campa: He is received into the lodge Alsace-Lorraine in Paris, a lodge named for the two provinces the peace treaty took away and made up largely of men who lost them. The name is the point. Around one table sit exiles from a territory that still exists on the ground and no longer exists in French law, and the sculptor of the Rapp monument is among them. Liberty is at this moment an unpaid idea in a Montparnasse studio, and the men who will subscribe to her in France are men of exactly this kind.
suggested_refs: The masonic lodge Alsace-Lorraine, Paris, joined 1875

stops.name: Paris, rue de Chazelles: the copper skin raised
stops.date_confidence: the workshop years 1876-1884 are attested by the NPS and en.wikipedia; month and day defaulted. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from gustave_eiffel.journey.json. That file flags an unresolved authorship question which is carried here unresolved: fr.wikipedia credits the skeleton's design to Maurice Koechlin working under Eiffel, en.wikipedia to Eiffel himself.
stops.campa: In a workshop yard in the seventeenth arrondissement the firm of Gaget, Gauthier et Cie builds the statue at full size, copper sheet hammered over wooden forms, a skin a few millimetres thick and forty six metres tall. Gustave Eiffel is brought in to solve what the sculptor cannot: an iron pylon with a flexible secondary frame, so the skin rides loose upon it and moves in frost and gale without tearing. Parisians watch a raised arm rise over the rooftops of the quarter years before the rest of her exists.
stops.quote: the system of hammered copper, which, from an artistic point of view, offers elements of excellence when it is well treated
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), on repousse copper as his medium, Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The Gaget, Gauthier et Cie yard at the rue de Chazelles, where the statue was built and test-assembled entire
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Philadelphia, Fairmount Park: the arm at the Centennial
stops.date_confidence: en.wikipedia 'Centennial Exposition' records the arm reaching Philadelphia only in August 1876, too late for the exhibition catalogue; the day is not given and is defaulted. The admission is corrected to fifty cents, on which en.wikipedia and es.wikipedia 'Estatua de la Libertad' agree independently. Coordinate is the exposition-grounds pin used elsewhere in the atlas for Fairmount Park.
stops.campa: The torch bearing arm, cast and shipped ahead of the body, reaches Fairmount Park in August, too late for the exhibition catalogue, and stands on the Centennial grounds as a giant hand holding fire with no woman attached to it. Fifty cents buys the ladder up to the balcony that rings the flame. It is the first piece of Liberty most Americans ever see, and it is shown in order to raise the money that will finish the rest of her. When the exposition closes in November the arm does not go home.
stops.quote: It will easily hold twelve persons.
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), on the torch platform, Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The torch and arm on the Centennial Exposition grounds, Fairmount Park, Philadelphia, 1876
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: New York, Union Square: Lafayette unveiled
stops.date_confidence: the 6 September 1876 dedication is attested by en.wikipedia, as is the execution in 1872 and the casting in 1873. Donor corrected: en.wikipedia 'Marquis de Lafayette (Bartholdi)' gives French residents of New York, an expatriate subscription, not a gift from the French people to the city. The stated motive, gratitude for American relief sent during the Franco-Prussian War, sits awkwardly with the centennial framing, and both readings are recorded without preference.
stops.campa: A bronze Lafayette offers his sword hilt first, the gesture of a Frenchman placing himself under an American command, and Bartholdi unveils it in Union Square in the centennial September. The subscription came from French residents of New York, an expatriate gift rather than a national one, and the motive they gave was gratitude for American relief sent to France during the late war. The marquis crossed at nineteen to fight for a republic that did not yet exist; the man modelling him has been carrying an unbuilt colossus for eleven years.
suggested_refs: Bartholdi's bronze Marquis de Lafayette, Union Square, New York, dedicated 6 September 1876
sources: New York City Parks Department monument records

stops.name: New York, Madison Square: the arm on the square
stops.date_confidence: the six-year stand in Madison Square and the 1882 return to France are attested by the NPS. The month is an inference from the Centennial's close on 10 November 1876 rather than a documented arrival date, and is flagged as such rather than defaulted.
stops.campa: The arm comes down from Fairmount Park and goes up again in Madison Square, where it stands for six years, a piece of civic furniture attached to nothing larger. New Yorkers walk past a copper hand the height of a house holding a flame over the grass, and subscriptions are taken at its foot. In 1882 it is dismantled and shipped back across the Atlantic to be joined at last to a body that has been growing without it in a yard on the rue de Chazelles.
suggested_refs: The torch and arm in Madison Square Park, New York, 1876-1882
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Newport, Rhode Island: the marriage at the city hall
stops.date_confidence: two contradictions, neither resolved. Place: fr.wikipedia specifies the hotel de ville of Newport, Rhode Island; en.wikipedia says Providence and is not corroborated, so Newport is preferred. Year: en.wikipedia gives 1876, while fr.wikipedia's 'la meme annee' attaches the 20 December date to 1884. 1876 is preferred only because it is compatible with his documented American stay, en.wikipedia 'Statue of Liberty' having him return to Paris in 1877. No contemporaneous record of the marriage was reached, and any claim that one exists is withdrawn.
stops.campa: He marries Jeanne Emilie Baheux de Puysieux at the city hall in Newport, on the twentieth of December, in the middle of an American fundraising campaign. There is no ceremony to speak of and no crowd, from a man who does most of his living on platforms in front of them. She becomes the companion of every journey after this one, Chicago in 1893 and the last rooms on the rue d'Assas included. The sources cannot agree which December it was, and the disagreement is left standing.
suggested_refs: Newport City Hall, Rhode Island, site of the marriage per fr.wikipedia

stops.name: Washington, Capitol Hill: the fountain installed
stops.date_confidence: 1878 installation at the base of Capitol Hill attested by en.wikipedia and USBG records; month and day defaulted. Corrections carried: cast by the Durenne foundry, not Val d'Osne; the lamps were originally gas and were replaced by electric globes later in the 1880s; the upper vasque is carried by three kneeling tritons, with nymphs below. The fountain was removed in 1926 and moved into the Botanic Garden only in 1932. Coordinate is en.wikipedia's 38.887127 / -77.012669, rounded.
stops.campa: A cast iron fountain shown at Philadelphia is bought by Congress for six thousand dollars and set at the base of Capitol Hill: three kneeling tritons holding up a basin, nymphs below, gas lamps burning over the water. The commission asks for pleasure rather than allegory, and he gives it. The lamps burn gas when it is built and are electric before the decade is out. It is pulled out in 1926 to make room for a war memorial and moved into the Botanic Garden in 1932, where it still throws water.
suggested_refs: The Bartholdi Fountain, United States Botanic Garden, Washington, D.C.
sources: United States Botanic Garden historical records

stops.name: Paris, Champ de Mars: the head at the Exposition
stops.date_confidence: attested by the NPS for the 1878 Exposition Universelle; month and day of the head's installation not established and defaulted. The measurements in the quote are Bartholdi's own, published 1885.
stops.campa: The head is finished before the body and goes on show at the Exposition Universelle, standing on the Champ de Mars with a stair inside it, so that visitors climb up through the neck and look out through the eyes and between the spikes of the crown. It is a fundraising instrument dressed as an exhibit. France has not finished paying for what it promised, America has not begun paying for the pedestal, and a face four metres tall in the middle of Paris is the argument put to both at once.
stops.quote: The head is 4.40 metres in height. The eye is .65 metres in width.
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The head of the Statue of Liberty exhibited at the Exposition Universelle, Champ de Mars, Paris, 1878
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history
Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (1885)

stops.name: Washington: the design patent D11,023
stops.date_confidence: the patent number and the year are attested by en.wikipedia and es.wikipedia 'Estatua de la Libertad'; filing and grant dates were not obtained and month and day are defaulted. The coordinate is the Old Patent Office Building and is a placement, not a record of where any transaction occurred.
stops.campa: He takes out an American design patent on the statue, number eleven thousand and twenty three, protecting the figure as a reproducible article at a moment when it is still an unfunded heap of copper in a Paris yard. He is forty five, the statue is seven years from standing, and he is already treating her as property. The instinct is commercial and it is correct: within a decade she is cast and sold in every size, from a mantelpiece ornament to a school facade, by foundries he does not control in cities he will never see.
suggested_refs: United States design patent D11,023, granted to Bartholdi for the Statue of Liberty

stops.name: Belfort: the lion below the citadel
stops.date_confidence: working dates contested and not resolved: en.wikipedia gives 1871-1880, fr.wikipedia gives 1875-1879. The 1880 completion per en.wikipedia is used for the pin and month and day are defaulted. Two corrections carried: the lion was assembled from separately carved red sandstone blocks, not cut from living rock, and it was designed to face east toward Prussia but reversed to face west to avoid provoking the German Empire. Coordinate from en.wikipedia, 47 deg 38 min 12 sec N, 6 deg 51 min 53 sec E.
stops.campa: Below the citadel of Belfort, the one eastern city that held its siege while Alsace fell around it, a lion of red sandstone is assembled block by carved block against the rock. Wounded, refusing to lie down, it is a defeat rendered as a posture. Designed to face east toward Prussia, it was turned west before completion so as not to provoke the German Empire, and only an arrow beneath its paw still points at the border. It is his largest work on French soil. He is drawing a woman with a torch for a foreign harbour at the same time.
suggested_refs: The Lion of Belfort, red sandstone, below the citadel

stops.name: Paris, rue de Chazelles: presented to Minister Morton
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia 'Statue of Liberty' gives the formal presentation to Ambassador Levi P. Morton in Paris on 4 July 1884. An earlier dating of this ceremony to 4 July 1880 is a four-year error and is retracted. A separate Morton ceremony, the driving of the first rivet, is dated 24 October 1881 by es.wikipedia, and is not this one. Coordinate inherited from gustave_eiffel.journey.json.
stops.campa: The statue stands complete in the yard on the rue de Chazelles, taller than the roofs around it, and is formally presented to Levi P. Morton, the American minister to France, on the fourth of July. The republic that paid for her hands her to the republic that will keep her. She comes down again immediately, into three hundred and fifty pieces and more than two hundred crates, because the object was never designed to stay standing where it was made. Nine years of building in that yard end with a ceremony and a dismantling.
stops.quote: The core of this truss work is formed by a sort of pylon which has four points of attachment. Each of these points is sustained by three bolted braces, fifteen centimetres in diameter
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), on the internal iron pylon engineered by Eiffel's firm, Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The completed statue standing in the rue de Chazelles yard, presented to Levi P. Morton, 4 July 1884
sources: Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (1885)

stops.name: Rouen: the Isère loaded
stops.date_confidence: the loading at Rouen in May 1885 and the figures of some 350 pieces in over 200 crates are attested by the NPS; the day is not given and is defaulted.
stops.campa: The pieces are carted to Rouen and loaded into the hold of the French naval frigate Isere, three hundred and fifty numbered fragments in more than two hundred crates. Nine years of hammering have turned a rejected Egyptian lighthouse into two hundred tons of copper and iron, and the last act of the work is watching it broken back down into freight. Nobody sees a statue again until Bedloe's Island. Between Rouen and New York she exists as a manifest and a set of numbers stencilled on wood.
suggested_refs: The frigate Isere loading the dismantled statue at Rouen, May 1885
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: New York Harbor: the Isère arrives
stops.date_confidence: attested by the NPS for 17 June 1885, including the crowd figure of some two hundred thousand. The coordinate is a harbour pin rather than a berth.
stops.campa: The Isere comes through the Narrows on the seventeenth of June and two hundred thousand people line the docks and the shore to watch a French warship deliver a dismantled goddess in crates. Fourteen years have passed since Bartholdi first sailed into this water with a watercolour and no money. The pedestal is still unfinished and still unfunded; the statue lands on the continent it was made for and waits in pieces on an island while a newspaper campaign raises the last of what her footing costs.
suggested_refs: The arrival of the Isere in New York harbour, 17 June 1885
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Paris: Commander of the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: the elevation in 1886 is attested by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia; no exact date was established, so month and day are defaulted and the stop is placed before the October dedication for that reason only, not because the order is known.
stops.campa: France makes him a Commander of the Legion of Honour. He is fifty two, and the decoration arrives in the year the largest object he will ever make finally stands where he intended it, on the far side of an ocean, in another country's harbour. The province he was born in still belongs to the German Empire. A man who cannot go home to Colmar as a Frenchman is honoured by the French state for a monument to another republic's liberty. The date within the year is not recorded in the sources reached here, only the year itself.
suggested_refs: Bartholdi's elevation to Commander of the Legion of Honour, 1886

stops.name: Liberty Island: the dedication in the fog
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia and the NPS agree on 28 October 1886 with President Cleveland presiding. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from gustave_eiffel.journey.json, which pins the same dedication. Bartholdi's age is corrected here to fifty two: born 2 August 1834, he was not sixty two, an error of ten years found in circulating accounts.
stops.campa: President Grover Cleveland presides on the twenty eighth of October, fifteen years after the sculptor walked this ground and picked it. Fog sits on the harbour so thickly that much of the ceremony is heard rather than seen, ships sounding to each other, a torch and a raised arm surfacing out of grey weather. Bartholdi is fifty two. The colossus he first drew for the mouth of the Suez Canal, refused by a khedive on grounds of cost, stands at the mouth of the Hudson instead and is not refused again.
stops.quote: It will represent 'Liberty Enlightening the World.' At night a resplendent aureole upon its brow will throw its beams far upon the vast sea.
stops.quote_source: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi, The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World (New York, 1885), Internet Archive statuelibertyen00bartgoog
suggested_refs: The dedication of Liberty Enlightening the World, Bedloe's Island, 28 October 1886
sources: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty history

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Barrancas de Belgrano: the cast iron Liberty
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved. en.wikipedia 'Replicas of the Statue of Liberty' gives 3 October 1886 and a base mark reading Val d'Osne, 8 Rue Voltaire, Paris, with the year 1884. es.wikipedia 'Barrancas de Belgrano' reports two candidate years, 1875 and 3 October 1886, cites neither and decides neither; 1875 would predate the New York statue entirely. The Bartholdi-mould attribution is fr.wikipedia's and is firm; the date is not. The foundry-mark wording was reached only through a summary and is not independently cross-checked.
stops.campa: Three metres of cast iron painted the colour of bronze stand on the bluffs above the Rio de la Plata, a Liberty raised in Buenos Aires from the same mould as one of the Paris casts, with the foundry mark of Val d'Osne of the rue Voltaire on her base and the year 1884. She goes up while the original is still being bolted together on an island eight thousand kilometres north. Argentine sources cannot agree on the year, and one of them offers 1875, which would set the copy eleven years before the thing it copies.
stops.quote: Petite réplique en fer réalisée par Bartholdi dans le même moule qu'une des répliques de Paris.
stops.quote_source: fr.wikipedia, 'Repliques de la statue de la Liberte', entry on Buenos Aires
suggested_refs: The cast-iron Liberty in Plaza Barrancas de Belgrano, Buenos Aires, and its Val d'Osne base mark
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Repliques de la statue de la Liberte'
en.wikipedia, 'Replicas of the Statue of Liberty'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Avenida Callao 450: the Liberty on the school facade
stops.date_confidence: attested by es.wikipedia for the Escuela Normal Superior n.9 Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, architect Carlos Morra, inaugurated 3 October 1886, twenty-five days before New York. Two corrections: the institution is not a Colegio Nacional Sarmiento, and the date is not 8 September. Note the finding this produces: the twenty-five-days formula demonstrably belongs to this school statue, not to the Barrancas de Belgrano cast that most repetitions attach it to. No source claims a direct Bartholdi hand in this particular casting.
stops.campa: On the facade of a new normal school on the Avenida Callao, Carlos Morra sets a second Liberty above the cornice, and the building opens on the third of October, twenty five days before New York. Argentina has two of her before the United States has one. The woman with the torch is by now an article of commerce as much as a monument, sold out of a Paris ironfoundry catalogue to school boards and municipalities, and Bartholdi, who never crosses to South America, does not need to be present for any of it.
suggested_refs: The Liberty on the facade of the Escuela Normal Superior n.9 Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, Avenida Callao 450, Balvanera
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Escuela Normal Superior n.9 Domingo Faustino Sarmiento'
en.wikipedia, 'Colegio Nacional de Buenos Aires' (checked, negative)

stops.name: Paris, Île aux Cygnes: the quarter scale bronze
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia 'Ile aux Cygnes' for the inauguration by President Sadi Carnot on 4 July 1889. Two corrections carried: the donors were the French expatriate community living in the United States giving to the city of Paris, not the American community in Paris, and the statue faced east toward the Eiffel Tower until it was turned west toward New York in 1937.
stops.campa: A quarter scale bronze goes up on a narrow made island in the Seine, given to the city of Paris by French people living in the United States, and inaugurated by President Sadi Carnot on the fourth of July for the centenary of the Revolution. She is set facing east, toward the new tower of Gustave Eiffel, and is turned west toward New York only in 1937, long after both men are dead. Parisians cross the footbridge past her daily. Most of them will never see the one in New York.
suggested_refs: The quarter-scale Liberty on the Ile aux Cygnes, Paris, inaugurated 4 July 1889
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Replicas of the Statue of Liberty'

segments.name: The Last Works and the Grave

stops.name: Chicago, Jackson Park: the White City
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia that Bartholdi visited the World's Columbian Exposition with his wife; no date within the season was established and month and day are defaulted.
stops.campa: He comes to the World's Columbian Exposition with Jeanne Emilie and walks the White City, a temporary capital of plaster built to look like marble, gigantism arranged by other men and applauded by millions. He is fifty nine. Liberty is seven years old in the harbour and known everywhere, and the visit has the shape of an elder's tour rather than a working trip. He first met American scale at Niagara in 1871. It has since learned to raise a whole city in plaster and take it down again in a season.
suggested_refs: The World's Columbian Exposition, Jackson Park, Chicago, 1893

stops.name: Clermont-Ferrand: Vercingetorix on horseback
stops.date_confidence: year attested by en.wikipedia; month and day of the inauguration not established and defaulted.
stops.campa: An equestrian Vercingetorix goes up at Clermont-Ferrand, the Gaulish chief who lost to Caesar raised on horseback by a century that lost Alsace to Prussia. It is the last of the great commissions and it makes the same argument as the lion at Belfort: a defeat can be given a posture that refuses it. He is sixty nine and ill. The public work that opened with a bronze Napoleonic general in his own town closes with a bronze chieftain from before France had a name to be defeated under.
suggested_refs: Bartholdi's equestrian Vercingetorix, Place de Jaude, Clermont-Ferrand

stops.name: Paris, 82 rue d'Assas: the death
stops.date_confidence: attested; fr.wikipedia gives 4 October 1904 at 82 rue d'Assas in the sixth arrondissement. Cause contested: fr.wikipedia gives only maladie, while en.wikipedia and several sketches name tuberculosis, and the difference is not settled here. Coordinate placed at the address, near 48.8437 / 2.3319; a circulating 48.8477 / 2.3299 falls roughly 450 m north by the Luxembourg and is discarded.
stops.campa: He dies at his flat on the rue d'Assas, in the sixth arrondissement, a few streets from the rue Vavin workshop he kept for forty years. He is seventy. The French sources say only that it was an illness; several later accounts name tuberculosis, and the difference is not settled. He leaves a widow and no children, and leaves the Colmar house to the town he was born in. The world's fairs that carried his whole career have moved on to steel and electric light, and the copper he worked in is already a period material.
suggested_refs: Bartholdi's last residence, 82 rue d'Assas, Paris 6e

stops.name: Paris, Montparnasse Cemetery: the grave in the 28th division
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Montparnasse in the 28th division, under an allegorical Renown co-sculpted with Auguste Rubin, is attested by fr.wikipedia; the exact day of interment was not established and is placed a few days after the death. Coordinate corrected: a circulating 48.8422 / 2.3266 falls outside the cemetery, up by the Tour Montparnasse.
stops.campa: He is buried in the twenty eighth division of the Montparnasse cemetery under an allegorical figure of Renown, cut with Auguste Rubin. No colossus marks the grave. The plot is an ordinary sculptor's plot among thousands, a short walk from the studio where the first small clay Liberties were modelled, before anyone in France had heard the name of Bedloe's Island. The largest thing he made stands eight thousand kilometres west of him, in the keeping of another country.
suggested_refs: Bartholdi's tomb, 28th division, Cimetiere du Montparnasse, with the Renown figure by Auguste Rubin

stops.name: Colmar, rue des Marchands: the house becomes a museum
stops.date_confidence: attested by fr.wikipedia and en.wikipedia: the house was bequeathed to Colmar in 1907 and opened as the Musee Bartholdi in 1922. Month and day of the opening not established and defaulted.
stops.campa: The house on the rue des Marchands, bequeathed to Colmar in 1907, opens as a museum under his name. Alsace has changed sovereign twice since he was carried out of this door as an infant and will change twice more within forty years. The rooms fill with maquettes, drawings, the Egyptian sketchbooks of 1855 and the working models of the woman with the torch. The town that commissioned his General Rapp at twenty two now shows visitors the room he was born in.
suggested_refs: The Musee Bartholdi, 30 rue des Marchands, Colmar, opened 1922

stops.name: Villa Aberastain, San Juan: the Liberty in Plaza Libertad
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia 'Villa Aberastain' gives the installation as 9 July 1931 in Plaza Libertad, formerly Plaza de Mayo, and records the plinth dates 1810-1910 with an Argentine shield. The France-donation attribution and the Federico Cantoni request are local testimony, presented in the source itself as an inference, and stay a reconstruction. An earlier reading of the 1931 date as marking a centenary is a garble and is retracted: the centenary in question is 1910. Coordinate is an approximate town placement, not a verified monument pin.
stops.campa: In a plaza in San Juan province, renamed Plaza Libertad, a Liberty is set up on the ninth of July, bearing the dates 1810 and 1910 and an Argentine shield. The local account holds that she was asked of France for the centenary of the May Revolution, was meant for a park in San Juan city, and arrived here twenty one years late by a mayor's decision. The dates on her plinth belong to a revolution she has nothing to do with, in a country the sculptor never saw and twenty seven years after he was dead.
suggested_refs: The Liberty of Plaza Libertad, Villa Aberastain, San Juan Province, installed 9 July 1931
sources: en.wikipedia, 'Replicas of the Statue of Liberty'
